editorNote: This week follows the Chronicle state file to May 2-8, 1983, when the home-computer aisle and the arcade aisle increasingly shared the same customers.
morningLine: Vector cockpits, spreadsheet desks, and discount home-computer ads all compete for attention in the first week of May 1983.

lead.headline: Star Wars lines up for Atari vector cabinets
lead.dek: Atari's Star Wars arcade machine gives the week its clearest computer-culture image: a 3-D vector trench run landing just as home computers borrow more of the arcade shelf.
lead.body: Trade and collector records place Atari's Star Wars arcade release in 1983, with May widely used for the cabinet's arrival. Its color-vector cockpit fantasy made a natural front-page emblem for a spring when home-computer owners were also buying arcade conversions, strategy disks, and BASIC-friendly machines from the same stores.
lead.confidence: High for 1983 release and period significance; medium for exact May-week placement.

computerItems.title: Commodore 64 keeps squeezing the home shelf
computerItems.summary: By spring 1983 the C64 had become a price-pressure machine: color graphics, SID sound, and falling street prices put it beside game cartridges, monitors, and cassette drives in mainstream ads.
computerItems.confidence: High for 1983 market position; medium for week-specific ad timing.

computerItems.title: IBM PC XT sets the office reference price
computerItems.summary: The March 1983 PC XT, with a 10 MB fixed disk, remained the machine to beat in office computing even while hobby columns watched cheaper home systems.

computerItems.title: Lotus 1-2-3 turns the PC into a spreadsheet desk
computerItems.summary: Lotus 1-2-3 was now the 1983 software name that explained why businesses were buying IBM-compatible desks instead of treating personal computers as experiments.

computerItems.title: Infocom adventures prove text still sells
computerItems.summary: Infocom's 1983 catalog, including Planetfall, kept parser adventures prominent on computer-store shelves while arcade licenses fought for attention.
computerItems.confidence: High for 1983 release; medium for exact week placement.

briefs.headline: Beat It holds the radio lead
briefs.text: Michael Jackson led the Billboard Hot 100 dated May 7, 1983, ahead of Dexys Midnight Runners and Thomas Dolby.

briefs.headline: Flashdance remains the film to catch
briefs.text: Flashdance was the dominant early-May box-office title, with Valley Girl and The Outsiders still part of the spring movie conversation.

briefs.headline: Famicom nears its Japanese debut
briefs.text: Nintendo's Family Computer was still weeks from its July 1983 launch, but the hardware path toward a new console era was forming.

briefs.headline: Text adventures stay printable
briefs.text: Infocom packaging and feelies gave computer games a bookstore-like presence that arcade cartridges could not copy.

periodAd.headline: Bring the arcade home, keep the ledger at work
periodAd.summary: One dealer window can sell a joystick, a spreadsheet, a disk drive, and a monitor to the same household this month.
periodAd.tagline: Computer Chronicle classifieds: software, modems, repairs, and used drives.

market.headline: The home-computer price war becomes the week's business story
market.summary: Commodore, Atari, Texas Instruments, and Apple were forcing shoppers to compare memory, color, keyboards, and software libraries as much as brand names.
market.confidence: High for 1983 trend; medium for exact week.

worldAnchor.headline: U.S. jobless rate dips to 10.2 percent
worldAnchor.summary: The Labor Department reported the U.S. unemployment rate fell to 10.2 percent in April 1983, a small but widely noted sign in the early Reagan-era recovery.
